Well first the conditions have to be right for life to form. We still don't know for sure what exactly that is. We do know that organic compounds and proteins can form naturally all the time. Scientists have created single celled organisms in labs trying to recreate the original conditions, but these artificially made critters do not last very long and cannot reproduce.

Over a period of about 2 billion years, the most basic chemical proteins merged together to make slightly more complex natural organic structures. Many of these merged together randomly over the first 2 billion years until a viable self replicating, self contained structure was formed. Think of the infinite monkeys with typewriters eventually writing Shakespeare. These creatures are known as prokaryotic cells and still exist today.

Over a period of about 2 billion more years, these little guys palled around, replicating (creating duplicate daughter cells identical to the original), mutating (one encounters conditions different from another, takes in different chemicals or substances that combine with its DNA causing an accidental chance change, or an error occurs while making the copy DNA) and even morphing together until eventually, one day, one prokaryote sort of swallowed a smaller one. But instead of breaking it down and digesting it, the smaller one sort of lived inside the bigger one from then on. No longer a single celled organism but now an organelle of the larger cell. This is how we have mitochondria in our cells to this day. (The DNA in your mitochondria is not the same as the DNA in the nucleus of your cells that makes you a human).

About a billion more years pass and one day, on accident (a lot of evolution happens by accident if you hadn't noticed) a cell fails to divide properly, resulting in a viable multi-cellular organism. Around this time I think is also when some cells begin to reproduce by exchanging DNA with other cells instead of exclusively through mitosis. This is where sex began and greatly accelerated the evolutionary process because now, instead of an organism splitting into two smaller identical copies, they produced a mutated morph of the two parent cells (like how each human is a mutant morph of their parents). So now every time two critters mated, you could never be sure exactly what you were going to get. The product is a potentially infinite amount of genetic offshoots, most of which were ill suited to the environment but some were in fact better suited to the environment (by chance of course). The ones that were better suited survived long enough to reproduce its own genetic offshoots, again most of them were crap but some were better than their parents. And so generation after generation it went on.

Fast forward about a half a billion more years, more complex multi-cellular life has formed (again mostly by accident), some capable of absorbing sunlight and converting it to energy, others with more mobility. I hope you can see where this is going. Keep going forward in time and eventually you have full blown macro organisms with complex organic structures like specialized organs that work in tandem to keep the larger complete organism alive.

The key thing to understand here is that the changes between generations is so small that you will never find a definite line between one organism and what it eventually turns into. This is a topic widely debated by anthropologists. We know we share a common ancestor with chimps, that one day long ago, there was a creature that was neither chimp nor man. One tribe went one way and the other tribe went another way. They no longer lived in the same conditions and the two tribes slowly diverged from each other. It is a gradual process with only man made boundaries between the eons of our past ancestors. What we do know is there are very large and measurable differences between the hominids of now, the hominids from 100,000 years ago, the hominids of 500,000 years ago and 1 million and 2 million years ago. But there is so much of the fossil record that is still incomplete (the conditions for creating fossils that last to now is much rarer than you would guess) that it would be difficult to say where the line is between what we would consider the "First Human" and the "Last Proto-Human". In a very real way, there is no first human, since our DNA can be traced all the way back to the very first viable cell.

TL;DR: Evolution happens over generations, not time. The cycle began by chance proteins combining in a self replicating form. The changes between each generation are so small that you cannot notice them unless you are looking at an ancestor and descendant that are at least a few hundred generations apart. What we call modern humans have only been around for about 500 generations or so.

To begin, the currently accepted theory of the origin of life from nothing, otherwise known as abiogenesis, is the RNA world hypothesis where basic replicators form out of short strands of RNA about 100 nucleotides long, though the scientific community is highly divided across a number of other different theories since each is riddled with their own shortcomings and strengths. Since the RNA world hypothesis has fewer issues within it than the others, it is often considered the most resilient, though it too has its share of shortcomings..

...the following objections have been raised to the RNA world hypothesis: (i) RNA is too complex a molecule to have arisen prebiotically; (ii) RNA is inherently unstable; (iii) catalysis is a relatively rare property of long RNA sequences only; and (iv) the catalytic repertoire of RNA is too limited.

To note, most experiments with the RNA world resemble chemical engineering far more than they represent any actual prebiotic genesis of life, seeing that to create these strands of nucleotides, pure samples of chemicals are used in clean environments, verses in the real world these would have had to formed in the messy per-biotic soup which would have had vastly lower concentrations of the desired chemicals. Keep in mind that evolution must take simple steps between forms, since the theory of evolution requires that mutations be selected one at a time because it otherwise would be completely improbable for them to happen at once.

As far as mutations go, the probability of a beneficial mutation within the space of all possible mutations is vanishingly small, such that it takes millions of generations to generate such a mutation. When that happens, the mutation happens in a random spot, and to create a functional segment of genes to code for something, then that would require hundreds of mutations within the same location, since genes are typically very long. Keep in mind, though, that for organisms, mutations are almost exclusively single nucleotide changes that happen at random spots in the DNA, so it is highly unlikely for a mutation to happen in a location that begets synergy with another mutation.

Now, focusing on species that have progressively longer generation times and smaller population sizes, we run into a series of problems, but most notably: 1) the mutation rate per generation does not scale with the length of generation, such that the net number of mutations decreases. 2) Species with small numbers of members have less of a chance (as a species) to generate mutations.

Now, let's look at what should be one of the fastest evolving species, malaria, since it has an exceedingly short generation time and an absolutely massive number of members (upwards of 10^10) at any given time. Since around the 70's-80's it has experienced upwards of 10^20 individual organisms that have lived and died. Assuming 1 mutation per generation, that leaves us at 10^20 possible mutations. Humanity in comparison, with its small population sizes and long generation times, even when alloted the time between the branch away from the rest of the pre-ape lines, has not experienced the huge population sizes of the malaria species. Being generous, let's double the number of people who have ever lived since 50,000bc to 200 billion to account for every member of the species and its ancestors (but to be frank the vast majority of the human line would have lived after 50,000bc). Each generation, an individual human will gain an additional 100 to 300 mutations, so being generous and assuming 300 mutations, that multiplies out to humanity experiencing 1.8*10^14 mutations in its history since the line broke away from the pre-apes.

During that time, humanity is supposed to have evolved multiple adaptations, ranging from bipedal locomotion to sentience which even human programmers have not managed to replicate. In comparison, if we look at Malaria, it has experienced magnitudes more mutations and much harsher selection than humanity ever has, yet we can verify that the most it has gained in that time are a handful of mutations which confer resistance to drugs - mutations which have been shown to only be a few nucleotides in size, and which break pre-existing systems. If the species were working under evolutionary expectations, then we would expect to see some massive changes in not only its genetics, but its physical form as well, since it has had 500,000x the number of mutation/section cycles humanity (and pretty much any slow generation species) has had. Yet nothing happened.

Also, before someone points out that malaria has only had 40 years to evolve, realize because of its large population size and quick generation times, malaria species has experienced a far greater chance for evolutionary change than humanity has ever had (I.E. mutation/selection events). In fact, this is exactly what the OP said "Evolution happens over generations, not time". In short, observing malaria for several decades can be considered the equivalent of watching a long generation species across multiple millions of years, yet comparing genetic samples of malaria from the 80's to modern times, there has been no notable changes.

This strongly hints that suggested evolutionary mechanisms are insufficient to account for the perceived change in species, since we would have expected to see some greater level of change in malaria in the last few decades since it has been given the same evolutionary resources as humanity.
